You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Pearl

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "The pearl primarily symbolizes the Kingdom of Heaven (or the salvation/gospel found in it) as a treasure of supreme, surpassing worth — something so valuable that a person should gladly give up everything else to obtain it. By extension it stands for sacred, precious spiritual truth.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Matthew 13:45-46 (the Parable of the Pearl of Great Price: the kingdom of heaven likened to a merchant who sells all he has to buy one pearl of great value)",
    "Matthew 7:6 ('do not cast your pearls before swine' — pearls as holy, precious truth not to be treated with contempt)",
    "Revelation 21:21 (the twelve gates of the New Jerusalem each made of a single pearl, associating pearls with the glory and worth of God's kingdom)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Christ himself as the pearl of great price — the believer surrenders everything to gain Christ (Phil 3:7-8 often cited in support).",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 13:45-46",
        "Philippians 3:7-8"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The reversed reading: the merchant is Christ and the pearl is the Church or the individual believer, whom Christ 'purchased' at the cost of everything (his life). Popular in some evangelical and dispensational teaching.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 13:45-46",
        "1 Corinthians 6:20",
        "Ephesians 5:25-27",
        "Acts 20:28"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Pearls as worldly luxury, ostentation, and moral corruption — adornment of the immodest or of 'Babylon the Great,' symbolizing wealth opposed to godliness.",
      "basis": [
        "1 Timothy 2:9",
        "Revelation 17:4",
        "Revelation 18:12-16"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Patristic/mystical readings of the pearl as the soul, purity, or the incarnate Word (e.g., the pearl formed in the oyster as an image of the virgin birth in some early Christian and Syriac writings such as Ephrem the Syrian's Hymns on the Pearl).",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 13:45-46 (allegorized)",
        "extrabiblical patristic tradition"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Gnostic-influenced reading of the pearl as the divine soul lost in the material world (as in the 'Hymn of the Pearl' from the Acts of Thomas) — sometimes referenced in scholarship but not mainstream Christian teaching.",
      "basis": [
        "Acts of Thomas (Hymn of the Pearl, extracanonical)"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is a broadly settled consensus that the pearl symbolizes something of supreme spiritual value — most commonly the Kingdom of Heaven/salvation per Matthew 13:45-46, with Matthew 7:6 supporting the sense of holy truth. The chief live interpretive debate concerns the parable's direction: whether the seeker is the believer (pearl = kingdom/Christ) or Christ (pearl = church/believer); both readings are widely taught. A distinct negative valence (pearls as luxury and worldliness) coexists in the New Testament and is recognized in standard commentaries, but it does not displace the dominant positive symbolism."
}

However, in the Epistles and Revelation, it frequently symbolizes corrupt earthly luxury and vanity, contrasted later by its use as the gates of the New Jerusalem, restoring its association with divine glory."
}

RESPONSE C

  "primary_meaning": "The pearl most commonly symbolizes the incomparable worth of the kingdom of God—and, by extension, salvation or life in Christ—worth surrendering everything else to obtain.",

      ],

      ],

    },
    {

      "basis": [

        "Revelation 18:12,16"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"

  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is a strong dominant association between pearls and exceptional spiritual preciousness, especially the supreme value of the kingdom in Matthew 13:45–46. However, there is no fully settled one-to-one symbolic referent across Scripture: context can make the pearl represent the kingdom, Christ, sacred truth, redeemed glory, or material luxury. Even within the pearl-of-great-price parable, interpreters differ over whether the pearl specifically represents the kingdom or Christ, and whether the merchant represents the seeker or Christ."
}

RESPONSE D

      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "The parable supplies the dominant Christian symbolic association; secondary uses (Matt 7:6; Rev 21) are also standard. Allegorical details of the parable (who is the merchant, what exactly is the pearl) vary by tradition but do not displace the core sense of supreme value."
}

BOOK ENTRY
The full moon — one complete light marking an appointed month and meeting at the east gate. The city's twelve pearl-gates correspond to the twelve months and bear the tribes' names.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: the kingdom worth everything, or the Church purchased by Christ.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Prov 3:15; 31:10; Ps 81:3; Prov 7:20; Job 26:9; Ps 104:19; Rev 21:21) · see The Pearls of Wisdom, ch. 31

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Proverbs 3:15 — She is more precious than rubies: and all the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her.
Proverbs 31:10 — Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies.
Psalms 81:3 — Blow up the trumpet in the new moon, in the time appointed, on our solemn feast day.
Proverbs 7:20 — He hath taken a bag of money with him, and will come home at the day appointed.
Job 26:9 — He holdeth back the face of his throne, and spreadeth his cloud upon it.
Psalms 104:19 — He appointed the moon for seasons: the sun knoweth his going down.
Revelation 21:21 — And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
